summary: Describes a method for compressing IPX datagram headers over wide area links, so less bandwidth goes to overhead. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1553 describes a way to shrink Novell's IPX packets on slow wide area links. The 30-byte header of an IPX packet stays the same for the whole life of a connection, so each end of the link stores it once in a table, and later packets name the table entry instead of repeating the header. What travels is usually one or two bytes rather than thirty.

questions: how does ipx header compression work
subtitle: Shrinking a 30-byte IPX header to one or two bytes on slow wide area links.

tldr.problem: On a slow wide area link, the fixed 30-byte header of every IPX packet is a large share of the traffic. Novell's IPX was used for file server access over such links, where that overhead cost real time.
tldr.mechanism: Both ends of the link keep a table of slots, each holding the full header of one connection. Because those headers never change during a connection, later packets carry only a one-byte flags field and, if needed, a slot number. A separate algorithm compresses the six-byte NCP header along with the IPX header.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1553 is Historic and the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was a standards track specification, and it sets out a compression ratio of about 2 to 1 for ordinary IPX traffic, with 15.50 in the best case of one byte of data and a one-byte header.

today: RFC 1553 is Historic, which means the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was a standards track specification produced by the Point-to-Point Protocol Extensions Working Group, and it has not been obsoleted by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why Compress IPX Headers
sections.content:
Internetwork Packet Exchange is a protocol defined by the Novell Corporation, derived from the Internet Datagram Protocol of the Xerox Network Systems family. IPX is a datagram, connectionless protocol that does not require an acknowledgement for each packet sent, and it corresponds to the network layer of the ISO model. A transport layer protocol usually sits above it: the Netware Core Protocol, used for file server access, and the Sequenced Packet Exchange, the reliable connection-based transport protocol commonly used by applications.

An IPX packet consists of a 30 octet header, usually followed by a transport layer header. The NCP header is 6 octets and the SPX header is 12 octets. Two compression strategies are described, and implementations of CIPX must support both. The first compresses only the IPX header, works with any IPX packet without affecting the transport protocol, and turns a 30 octet header into one to seven octets. The second compresses the combined IPX and NCP headers, applies only to NCP packets of type 0x2222 and 0x3333, and turns a 36 octet NCP/IPX header into one to eight octets. Both algorithms are based on the ones Van Jacobson described for TCP/IP packets.

Header compression can also be combined with data compression, which may take the form of link bit stream compression, normally performed by modems transparently, or transparent bit stream compression offered by some data service units, routers and bridges, or protocols such as CCITT V.42bis, MNP 5, Lempel-Ziv or LAPB. The order matters. When sending packets, data compression must be done after header compression, and when receiving packets, data decompression must be done before header decompression.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IPX packet starts with 30 bytes of header, and on a slow link that fixed cost is a large part of the packet. The header is also almost identical for every packet of a connection, so it can be stored once at each end and referred to afterwards. The rules also fix the order when header and data compression are used together: compress the header first, compress the data second, and undo it in the opposite order.

sections.title: What the IPX Header Hides
sections.content:
The normal IPX header holds a checksum, a packet length, a transport control field that counts hops, a packet type, and destination and source address fields. The checksum field has historically not been used by Novell, which required it to be set to 0xFFFF, and since it stays constant its value can be compressed away. Where checksums are implemented, the checksum must be included in the compressed packet, because recalculating it would destroy the end-to-end reliability of the connection; the memo notes that checksums are now implemented in the Fault Tolerant Servers.

For most links the packet length can be determined from the MAC layer. There are cases where it cannot, for example when hardware pads packets to a required minimum length, and on those links the length has to be included. The transport control field usually does not change between two end points, so compression assumes that it never changes and does not examine it when determining a connection. The packet type field is constant for any connection.

The destination and source address fields are each 12 octets, made up of a network field of 4 octets, a node field of 6 octets and a socket field of 2 octets. An IPX connection is the logical association between two endpoints known by a given source and destination address pair, and for any specific connection those address fields are constant. The fields that may therefore need to be included in the compressed header are the checksum and the packet length.

While IPX header compression is in use, packets can be lost, and the loss of an Initial packet is a problem, because if the sender later sends a compressed packet the receiving end cannot decompress it correctly. The IPX header does not carry enough information to detect a retransmission, so the sender of an Initial packet must be guaranteed that the packet has been received. The specification therefore provides a mechanism for confirmation of an Initial packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the IPX header does not change while a connection is running. The checksum is normally a fixed value, the length can often be worked out from the link, the hop count is assumed steady, the packet type is fixed, and the two addresses never change. That leaves the checksum and the length as the only fields that may have to be sent. The one thing that cannot be recovered is a lost first packet, because the header carries no way to detect a repeat, so the first packet has to be acknowledged.

sections.title: The CIPX Header and Its Packet Types
sections.content:
IPX compression must be negotiated by some means, for example IPXCP or IPXWAN. Each end must negotiate the desired options, such as the maximum number of concurrent connections maintained in each direction. Once compression is negotiated, all IPX packets sent over that link carry a CIPX header at the beginning of the packet. The CIPX header is variable in length, and the one octet header is added even when a regular IPX packet is sent over the link, so that CIPX can run over various WAN links as if they were normal IPX packets, without relying on any new link specific packet demultiplexing.

Both ends maintain send and receive tables holding the state of each connection. The original header for each connection is stored in a slot, typically one slot per client-server connection, and both sides keep a copy of the full IPX header for each slot. The sending side, the compressor, uses this to work out which fields have changed; the receiving side, the decompressor, uses it to rebuild the original packet header. The CIPX packet header specifies the type of the packet and any options for that packet, and its minimum length is one octet.

The low order four bits of that octet give the packet type. A Compressed packet has a lowest bit of zero, and the other packet types are odd numbers: 0 Compressed, 1 Regular, 3 Confirmed Initial, 5 Confirm, 7 Unconfirmed Initial and 9 Reject, with 11 to 15 reserved. The upper four bits are Packet Type Dependent Flags, which differ by packet type, and all bits that are reserved or not specified must be set to zero.

The flags octet must not contain the value 0xFF, so that a CIPX flags octet can be told apart from a normal IPX header with a 0xFFFF checksum field. That matters because with some link layer protocols, such as X.25 Permanent Virtual Circuits, one end of the link may fail and start sending regular IPX packets without the CIPX header; CIPX implementations must recognise this situation and renegotiate the use of CIPX. Any future expansion must ensure that at least one bit of the flags octet stays zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet on a compressed link starts with one byte. The bottom four bits say what kind of packet it is, and the top four bits hold flags that depend on that kind. A value of 0xFF is never used, so a receiver can always tell a compressed link from an ordinary IPX packet, which matters because one end of a link may start sending ordinary packets after a failure.

sections.title: The Optional Fields of a Compressed Packet
sections.content:
A Compressed packet contains no packet header at all, neither the 30 byte IPX header nor the 36 byte NCP header. A slot number tells the receiver which saved header to use to rebuild the original before passing the packet up to IPX. Each optional field is controlled by a flag, and when a field is present it appears in the same order in the compressed packet header, starting from the high order bits and working down.

The slot number field is one octet and names the slot that corresponds to the Initial packet header. Slots are numbered from zero to the maximum number of slots minus one. By default, slot compression is disabled, meaning the slot number is omitted and the same slot as the last packet is used. Slot compression may be enabled for slots created by an Unconfirmed Initial packet, but only in a receiver that can account for all erroneous and discarded packets: once a packet is discarded the slot number is indeterminate for later packets, and the decompressor must discard all further packets until a slot number is received.

The checksum flag, when set, includes the 2 octet checksum in the compressed packet; when clear, the decompressor assumes the checksum is 0xFFFF. The length flag includes the IPX data length field, which gives the length of the header and data in the packet before compression and does not include the CIPX compression fields. It is preferable to determine the length from the MAC layer whenever possible. Since every octet matters on a slow link, the length is written in one, two or three octets: one octet for a length of 0 to 127, two octets for 128 to 16383, and three octets above that, with the first octet holding 192 to mark the three octet form. The task number flag includes the NCP task number, which otherwise stays the same as in the last packet.

The minimum compressed IPX header contains only the flags octet, with the value 0x00, and all the fields of the original header are compressed out of it. The maximum compressed IPX header can include up to 7 octets: the flags, the slot number, the 2 octet checksum and the 3 octet length, or 8 octets if the NCP task number is included. The minimum and maximum packets are drawn in the memo with the flags values 0x00, 0xE0 and 0xF0.
sections.plainLanguage: A compressed packet carries no header of its own. Instead it names a slot, and the receiver rebuilds the header from what it has stored there. Only the fields that actually change are added back: the checksum when it is not the usual value, the length when the link cannot supply it, and the NCP task number when it changes. So the common case is a single byte.

sections.title: Negotiating Compression over PPP and IPXWAN
sections.content:
For PPP links, the use of header compression can be negotiated by IPXCP, and by default no compression is enabled. The IPX-Compression-Protocol configuration option indicates the ability to receive compressed packets, and each end of the link must separately request the option if bidirectional compression is wanted. The PPP Protocol field is set to the same value as for usual IPX packets, and all IPX packets sent over the link must conform to the compressed format. The option has type 3 and length 6, with an IPX-Compression-Protocol field of 0002 in hex for Telebit Compressed IPX headers, a one octet Max-Slot-Id field that is one less than the actual number of slots, and a one octet Options field. The options are 0 for no options, 1 for the slot identifier being compressed, and 2 for redefining bits 1 to 3 of the Compressed packet type. The slot identifier must not be compressed if there is no ability for the PPP link level to indicate an error in reception to the decompression module, because synchronisation after errors depends on receiving a packet with the slot identifier.

IPXWAN is the protocol Novell uses to exchange necessary router to router information before exchanging standard IPX routing information and traffic over WAN datalinks. To negotiate the Telebit compression option, Novell's allocated option number for CIPX is used in the IPXWAN timer request and response packet, with a WOption Number of 80 and a WOption Data length of 00 03. The option data carries the compression type, the compression options, and the number of compression slots.

IPX packets other than IPXWAN packets are not sent over the link until the IPXWAN negotiations are complete. If both ends agree on the compression options, the IPX packets are sent using the specified options; if either end does not accept an option, that option will not be used and compression proceeds with whatever remains. Implementations must support CIPX without any options. The Timer Response must contain a subset of the options received in the Timer Request, and it is the responsibility of the router sending that response to inform the other router of the options that will be used. IPXWAN sets up a symmetrical compression link: compression is configured identically in both directions, each end uses the same number of slots and the same options, and it is illegal for the link ends to use a different number of slots or different options.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression has to be agreed before it is used. Over PPP the two ends negotiate it in the IPXCP options, each asking for the ability to receive compressed packets. Over Novell's IPXWAN the same thing happens in the timer request and response. The link is set up symmetrically: both directions use the same number of slots and the same options, and if the ends cannot agree on an option it is simply not used.

sections.title: Compression Ratio and Security
sections.content:
The performance of the algorithm depends on the number of active connections and the number of slots negotiated. If there are more slots than connections, the hit rate should be very high and the compression ratio very good. Performance also depends on the average size of the IPX packets: the smaller the average packet, the more noticeable the improvement. The compression ratio is the average data length plus the uncompressed header length, divided by the average data length plus the average compressed header length, where the uncompressed header length is fixed at 30 octets, the minimum compressed header is 1 octet, and the maximum compressed NCP/IPX header is 8 octets including the NCP task number, though since no implementation yet sends packets longer than 16K, 7 octets is the commonly encountered maximum. A reasonable average compressed header length is 2, assuming the flags and slot number octets.

The maximum length of data in an IPX packet is 546 octets, being 576 octets less the 30 octet IPX header, although newer implementations may send packets of up to 4096 octets, and the minimum is 1 octet. Within the normal distribution of small NCP packets, a reasonable average data length is 26 octets. That gives a minimal compression of 1.04, a maximal compression of 15.50 and a likely compression of 2.00.

The Security Considerations section says that IPX provides some security features, which are fully applicable to CIPX, and that CIPX does not significantly alter the basic security of IPX.
sections.plainLanguage: How much the scheme saves depends on the size of the packets. With a typical short NCP packet of 26 bytes of data and a two-byte compressed header, the ratio is about two to one. With one byte of data and a one-byte header the best case is 15.50 to one. The memo also notes that compression does not change the security properties of IPX, since the security features IPX has apply just as well to the compressed form.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Normally 0xFFFF, so it can be left out.

fields.name: Packet Length
fields.desc: Often derivable from the MAC layer, so it can be left out.

fields.name: Hops
fields.desc: Transport control; assumed never to change.

fields.name: Destination Address
fields.desc: 12 octets: network, node and socket. Constant for the connection.

fields.name: Source Address
fields.desc: 12 octets: network, node and socket. Constant for the connection.

viz.caption: THE CIPX PACKET TYPES, FROM THE LOW ORDER BITS

items.label: Compressed
items.desc: No header is sent; a slot number says which saved header to use.

items.label: Regular
items.desc: An ordinary IPX packet with the one octet CIPX header removed.

items.label: Confirmed Initial
items.desc: Sends the full header for a slot and asks for confirmation.

items.label: Confirm
items.desc: Acknowledges a Confirmed Initial packet. Three octets long.

items.label: Unconfirmed Initial
items.desc: Sends the full header for a slot without asking for confirmation.

items.label: Reject
items.desc: Tells the sender the header is not supported. Three octets long.

items.label: Not a CIPX type
items.desc: Must be read as an ordinary IPX header and passed on.
